question:
Demographics: 43-year-old male
Chief Complaint: painful skin mass on the neck
History of Present Illness: Four days ago the patient noticed a painful lump on his neck that kept him awake at night. The lesion measured approximately 5 cm × 7 cm, contained pus in the center, and was surrounded by erythema and swelling. He denied fever throughout the course.
Past Medical History: penicillin allergy; no known chronic diseases
Physical Exam Findings: skin mass on neck approximately 5 cm × 7 cm; central purulent drainage; surrounding erythema; local swelling
Lab Findings: leukocyte count 18.2 × 10⁹/L

Demographics: 57-year-old male
Chief Complaint: persistent low mood, anxiety, and active suicidal thoughts for three weeks
History of Present Illness: The patient has a long-standing history of epilepsy and left-sided weakness after a right-sided traumatic brain injury sustained decades earlier. He previously underwent three craniotomies for right-sided subdural hematomas, the most recent five years ago. Follow-up imaging three years after the last surgery showed a small subacute subdural collection that was managed non-operatively. Over the preceding three weeks he experienced worsening low mood, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts, leading to a psychiatric admission. While hospitalized, a non-contrast MRI was performed because of his prior surgical history and demonstrated a 1.4 × 2.3 × 3.6 cm right-sided crescent-shaped collection consistent with a subacute subdural hematoma, without significant restricted diffusion. He was transferred to our facility, remained at his neurologic baseline, afebrile, and with a normal white blood cell count on arrival. Approximately 21 hours after admission, he was taken to the operating room for evacuation of the presumed subdural collection. Intraoperatively, the surgical field revealed unexpected purulent material in the epidural space and infected bone, which were removed. Post-operatively he exhibited a transient rise in white blood cell count, elevated inflammatory markers, and a single low-grade temperature, but remained neurologically stable and his psychiatric symptoms resolved by postoperative day 5. He was discharged to rehabilitation after 13 days and later underwent cranioplasty with a PEEK implant.
Past Medical History: epilepsy; left hemiplegia secondary to right traumatic brain injury; multiple prior craniotomies for right subdural hematoma
Exposures/Risk Factors: history of multiple cranial surgeries; prior traumatic brain injury
Physical Exam Findings: afebrile on presentation; normal white blood cell count on admission; neurologic status at baseline; no focal neurologic deficits
Lab Findings: White blood cell count within normal limits on admission; Elevated white blood cell count observed through postoperative day 3; Elevated C-reactive protein throughout admission; Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate throughout admission; Temperature 99.5 °F on morning of procedure
Imaging Findings: Non-contrast head CT after prior craniotomy showed a small subacute subdural hematoma; MRI (non-contrast) demonstrated a right-sided crescent-shaped collection measuring 1.4 × 2.3 × 3.6 cm, interpreted as subacute subdural hematoma; Diffusion-weighted images showed no significant restricted diffusion; MRI performed three months after cranioplasty showed no abnormal findings
Image Findings:
Image 1: An axial non-contrast CT scan of the head shows a crescent-shaped, hypodense collection along the right cerebral hemisphere, exerting mass effect with a midline shift to the left and compression of the right lateral ventricle. The lateral ventricles are symmetrically enlarged. A small, hyperdense focus is visible within the collection posteriorly. A linear, high-density artifact is present on the left side of the image frame.
Image 2: An axial MRI slice of the head shows a crescent-shaped, hyperintense collection along the right convexity, located between the inner table of the skull and the brain parenchyma. This collection exerts a mass effect, causing a leftward shift of the midline structures and compression of the right cerebral hemisphere. A small letter 'a' is visible in the bottom left corner of the image.
Image 3: An axial T2-weighted MRI of the head shows a large, biconvex, hyperintense extra-axial collection along the right convexity, which exerts a mass effect on the underlying brain parenchyma and causes a midline shift to the left. The cerebral ventricles are compressed, and the sulci are effaced on the right side. A small white letter "b" is located in the bottom left corner of the image.
Image 4: An axial MRI slice of the head shows a crescent-shaped, hyperintense collection located between the skull and the brain surface on the right side. This collection exerts a mass effect, causing a midline shift of the brain parenchyma toward the left. The brain tissue exhibits normal sulcal and gyral patterns elsewhere, and no annotations are present in the image.

Demographics: 45-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Irregular asymmetric nontender lump adjacent to the medial aspect of the left areola with slight nipple retraction, present for 6 months
History of Present Illness: The patient noticed an irregular, asymmetric, non-tender mass near the medial edge of the left areola about six months ago. The lesion has persisted without pain and is associated with mild retraction of the nipple. Over time, a palpable node developed in the left axilla. No systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or malaise were reported. He sought evaluation in a cytology outpatient department, where fine-needle aspiration was performed on both the breast mass and the axillary node.
Physical Exam Findings: Irregular, asymmetric, non-tender lump adjacent to the medial aspect of the left areola; Slight retraction of the left nipple; Palpable left axillary lymph node
Lab Findings: Fine-needle aspirate from the breast mass yielded 2 mL of pus-like material; Cytology smears showed numerous polymorphonuclear neutrophils, lymphocytes, macrophages, multinucleated foreign-body-type giant cells, nuclear debris, capillary fragments, and anucleated squames; no ductal epithelial cells were identified; Ziehl-Neelsen stain negative for acid-fast bacilli; Periodic acid-Schiff stain negative for fungal elements; Cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) showed no growth after 4 days; Blood glucose within normal limits; HIV serology negative
Imaging Findings: Ultrasound of the left breast demonstrated a 3 cm heterogeneous lesion containing multiple hypoechoic areas and internal moving echoes; Mild increase in peripheral vascularity on color Doppler; Right breast appeared normal on sonography
Image Findings:
Image 1: A clinical photograph of a person's chest showing the right pectoral region. There is a visible protrusion of the breast tissue beneath the nipple and areola. A small white letter "a" is located in the bottom left corner of the image.
Image 2: An ultrasound image showing a heterogeneous, predominantly hypoechoic mass with internal hyperechoic foci. The mass is irregularly shaped and situated within soft tissue. A lowercase white letter "b" is located in the bottom left corner of the image.
Image 3: A photomicrograph of a tissue section with a purple-toned stain. The image shows a background of densely packed cells and amorphous material, interspersed with several distinct, rounded, pale-staining structures with darker peripheral borders. A white letter 'c' is located in the bottom-left corner of the image.
Image 4: A photomicrograph showing a histological section stained with a blue-purple dye. The image displays numerous small, round inflammatory cells scattered throughout the field, interspersed with elongated, branching, filamentous structures. In the upper right quadrant, there is a larger, irregularly shaped cellular cluster containing a pinkish-red area. A small white letter "d" is located in the bottom left corner of the image.

Demographics: 70-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Weakness in the right arm, loss of dexterity, and gait disturbance for one month
History of Present Illness: The patient experienced progressively worsening weakness of the right arm, reduced manual dexterity, and difficulty walking over a period of one month, prompting evaluation. Initial cervical spine decompression surgery at C3-C5 led to temporary symptom improvement. Four days post-operatively he developed sudden neck pain accompanied by new motor weakness and decreased sensation in all four limbs. Several weeks later he reported pain in his left knee.
Past Medical History: Hypertension; Hypercholesterolemia
Exposures/Risk Factors: Recent cervical spine surgery (laminectomy); Immunocompetent status; No oral antithrombotic medication
Physical Exam Findings: Weakness of right upper extremity; Loss of dexterity in right hand; Gait disturbance; Acute neck pain; Motor deficit in all four limbs; Hypoesthesia in all four limbs; Pain in left knee
Lab Findings: Coagulase-negative staphylococci isolated from epidural exudate culture; Weakly birefringent basophilic crystals observed in hematoxylin and eosin–stained epidural material; Weakly birefringent basophilic crystals identified in left knee joint aspirate
Imaging Findings: MRI showed cervical spinal canal stenosis at C3/4 and C4/5 without ossification of posterior longitudinal or ligamentum flavum; no instability; Post-operative MRI demonstrated a well-demarcated dorsal epidural lesion at C6-C7, low signal on T1-weighted images and homogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images
Image Findings:
Image 1: A sagittal T2-weighted MRI of the cervical spine. The vertebral bodies are labeled with white text from C3 to C7. There is a focal area of high signal intensity within the spinal cord at the C5-C6 level, associated with a posterior protrusion of the intervertebral disc that narrows the spinal canal.
Image 2: A sagittal MRI of the cervical spine shows the C3 through C7 vertebrae. White text labels identify the vertebral bodies from C3 to C7. Three white arrowheads point to a region of abnormal signal intensity and tissue expansion posterior to the C5, C6, and C7 vertebral bodies, extending into the posterior elements of the spine.
Image 3: A sagittal MRI of the cervical spine shows the C3 through C7 vertebrae. Three white arrows point to a hyperintense, elongated mass located posterior to the C5, C6, and C7 vertebral bodies, which is causing anterior displacement and compression of the spinal cord. The mass is adjacent to a larger, heterogeneous, hyperintense region in the posterior soft tissues.

Demographics: 39-year-old male
Chief Complaint: fever and fatigue for 2 weeks
History of Present Illness: Two weeks prior to admission the patient developed a fever up to 38.8 °C, accompanied by occasional upper and middle abdominal pain and a cough producing thick, brick-red sputum. He denied chills. Initial treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics, liver-protective agents, and glucose control provided little relief, and his condition worsened with rising inflammatory markers, decreasing arterial oxygen tension, and a falling oxygenation index. He required transfer to an intensive care unit. Physical examination revealed tachypnea, coarse breath sounds with moist rales bilaterally, and right upper quadrant tenderness. Imaging demonstrated fluid-filled lesions in the right hepatic lobe, bilateral pulmonary consolidations with cavitary changes, and an enlarged prostate with low-density foci. Cultures from respiratory and hepatic samples grew Gram-negative organisms. Despite escalation of antimicrobial therapy and percutaneous drainage procedures, the lesions improved only gradually, prompting adjustments in antibiotics and repeat imaging. Over the subsequent weeks, serial CT scans showed progressive resolution of the hepatic and pulmonary lesions and partial improvement of the prostatic lesion, leading to discharge in a stable condition.
Past Medical History: long-standing diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycemic agents
Exposures/Risk Factors: diabetes mellitus
Physical Exam Findings: temperature 37.6 °C; pulse 133 beats/min; blood pressure 130/68 mmHg; conscious, emaciated appearance; tachypnea; coarse breath sounds bilaterally with moist rales; soft abdomen with right upper quadrant tenderness, no rebound; normal bowel sounds; no lower-extremity edema
Imaging Findings: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: hypodense fluid-filled lesion in the right hepatic lobe; Chest CT: bilateral pulmonary consolidations with cavitary components, showing progression on initial imaging and gradual improvement on follow-up scans; PET-CT: low-density hepatic lesion post-drainage; enlarged prostate with decreased attenuation suggesting inflammatory change; Follow-up CT after antimicrobial therapy: reduction in size of hepatic and pulmonary lesions, persistent low-density area in the prostate
Image Findings:
Image 1: Three axial CT images of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis are shown. The left image, displayed in lung window, shows a rounded, hyperdense nodule in the right upper lobe of the lung. The middle image, displayed in soft tissue window, shows the liver and spleen, with a small, hyperdense, curvilinear structure in the right lobe of the liver. The right image shows an axial view of the pelvis. Yellow 'L' and 'R' markers indicate the left and right sides of the patient, and a centimeter scale is visible on the right side of each image.
Image 2: Three axial CT images of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis are shown. The chest image displays bilateral, multifocal, patchy areas of increased opacity within the lung parenchyma. The abdominal image shows a large, heterogeneous, low-attenuation area within the liver and a small amount of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. The pelvic image shows the pelvic girdle and soft tissues. Each image includes orientation markers for right (R), left (L), and posterior (P), as well as a centimeter scale on the right side.
Image 3: Three axial CT images of a patient. The leftmost image shows a chest section with bilateral pulmonary opacities and multiple cavitary lesions. The middle image shows an abdominal section with a large, homogeneous, low-attenuation mass occupying a significant portion of the abdominal cavity. The rightmost image shows a pelvic section with a well-circumscribed, rounded soft-tissue mass located anterior to the pubic symphysis. Yellow 'L' and 'R' markers indicate the left and right sides of the patient, and a centimeter scale is visible on the right side of the abdominal and pelvic images.
Image 4: Three axial CT scan slices of a patient's torso are shown. The leftmost image is a chest CT in lung window, showing bilateral pulmonary opacities and cavitary lesions in the lower lobes. The middle image is an abdominal CT showing a large, heterogeneous, hypodense mass occupying a significant portion of the liver. The rightmost image is a pelvic CT showing the pelvic girdle and soft tissues. Yellow 'L' and 'R' markers indicate left and right orientation, and a centimeter scale is visible on the right side of each slice.

Demographics: 69-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Slight bloody sputum for seven days and a 5 kg weight loss over the past six months.
History of Present Illness: The patient noted the onset of slight bloody sputum approximately one week ago, accompanied by a gradual weight loss of about 5 kg over the preceding six months. He denied fever, cough, or shortness of breath. On admission his vital signs were within normal limits and he was afebrile. Physical examination showed clear lung sounds without respiratory distress. Laboratory testing demonstrated a leukocytosis (WBC 12,700 cells/µL) and an elevated C-reactive protein (14.76 mg/dL). Serial chest radiographs performed every three months for dialysis monitoring had shown progressive interstitial infiltrates over the prior six months. A chest CT performed on admission revealed multiple bilateral consolidations containing cavitary areas.
Past Medical History: diabetes mellitus; chronic kidney disease; hemodialysis-dependent renal failure
Exposures/Risk Factors: maintenance hemodialysis; regular chest imaging for dialysis monitoring
Physical Exam Findings: afebrile; normal vital signs; no respiratory distress; clear breath sounds bilaterally; unremarkable other physical examination findings
Lab Findings: WBC 12,700 cells/µL; CRP 14.76 mg/dL
Imaging Findings: Chest X-rays over the past six months showed multiple interstitial infiltrates; Chest CT on admission demonstrated multiple bilateral consolidations with cavitary components
Image Findings:
Image 1: A photomicrograph of a tissue sample stained with a pink-colored stain, likely PAS or similar, showing a background of amorphous eosinophilic material and several large, pale cells. Two black arrows point to small, oval, clear structures with a distinct outer wall. The image shows a high-magnification view of these small oval bodies interspersed among larger cellular elements.
Image 2: A grayscale image of an agarose gel electrophoresis result showing four vertical lanes containing multiple horizontal bands of varying intensity and position. The first and third lanes contain a higher number of bands, resembling a molecular weight ladder. The second and fourth lanes show a similar pattern of fewer, distinct bands. On the right edge of the image, several short, black horizontal tick marks are present, aligned with some of the bands.

Demographics: 82-year-old woman
Chief Complaint: recurrent fever for more than 10 days
History of Present Illness: Ten days before admission the patient developed urinary frequency, urgency and fever with chills, reaching 39.5 °C, without dysuria. She self-treated with antipyretics. Three days prior to admission she again had high fever (up to 40 °C) accompanied by chills, episodes of unconsciousness, fatigue and nausea (no vomiting). Lower abdominal pain was present, but no diarrhea, dizziness or headache. She presented to the emergency department and received intravenous ceftriaxone, which was escalated to imipenem/cilastatin after persistent fever. After transfer to our ward the fever subsided with continued antimicrobial therapy.
Physical Exam Findings: Temperature 36 °C; Pulse 63 bpm; Respiratory rate 18 breaths/min; Blood pressure 120/51 mmHg; Coarse breath sounds, no rhonchi or moist rales; Cardiac exam: no murmurs; Mild tenderness in lower abdomen, no rebound or guarding; No other abnormal findings
Lab Findings: White blood cell count 16.3 ×10^9/L; Neutrophils 90.4%; C-reactive protein 78.3 mg/L; Procalcitonin 1.67 ng/mL; Albumin 32 g/L; C-reactive protein 39.1 mg/L on day 16; Procalcitonin 0.116 ng/mL on day 16
Imaging Findings: Chest CT: subpleural patches in the lower dorsal lobe, considered related to a sagging effect; Abdominal CT (initial): splenomegaly, low-density lesion in the spleen, kidney cysts, minimal perinephric exudation, bladder wall thickening with a small amount of gas; cystitis could not be excluded; Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT (day 5): splenomegaly with a smaller low-density lesion in the spleen, multiple peripheral honeycomb-like weakly enhancing low-density areas; Abdominal CT (day 16): reduced size of the splenic low-density lesion with a small amount of gas in and around the spleen
Image Findings:
Image 1: Three axial CT images of the upper abdomen show the liver and spleen. In the spleen, there is a well-defined, low-attenuation, rounded lesion. The rightmost image shows a high-attenuation, linear, metallic-appearing object within the splenic parenchyma, adjacent to the low-attenuation area. No annotations are present on the images.
Image 2: An axial contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen shows the kidneys, aorta, and surrounding viscera. The right kidney exhibits a heterogeneous appearance with areas of decreased enhancement compared to the left kidney. A fluid-filled structure, consistent with the gallbladder, is visible in the right upper quadrant. No annotations or labels are present in the image.
Image 3: An axial CT scan of the pelvis shows the hip joints, bladder, and surrounding soft tissues. The femoral heads are positioned within the acetabula. A scale bar on the right side of the image indicates a total length of 19 cm. No annotations are present in the image.

Demographics: 3-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Right upper quadrant pain, fever, diarrhea, and nausea for three days
History of Present Illness: The child developed right upper quadrant discomfort associated with fever, diarrhea, and nausea that began three days prior to admission. There was no reported jaundice, prior abdominal surgery, or trauma. Symptoms progressed to include a palpable epigastric mass that was slightly tender, but without signs of peritonitis.
Physical Exam Findings: Temperature 38.2°C; Pulse 84 beats/min; Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg; Palpable epigastric mass, slightly tender; No peritoneal signs
Lab Findings: White blood cell count 19,500/mL with 75% polymorphonuclear leukocytes; C-reactive protein 130 mg/dL; Liver function tests within normal limits; Electrolytes within normal limits
Imaging Findings: Abdominal radiography unremarkable; Ultrasound: anechoic lesion measuring 5 × 4 cm in the left lobe of the liver; biliary ducts, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen normal; CT scan: 4 × 3 cm mass in the left lobe of the liver with surrounding inflammatory changes, extension into the overlying anterior abdominal wall, strongly enhanced peripheral margin, no internal enhancement
Image Findings:
Image 1: An axial contrast-enhanced CT scan of the upper abdomen. The image shows the liver, both kidneys, and the pancreas. There is a heterogeneous, low-attenuation area in the region of the pancreatic tail and peripancreatic space on the left side of the image, associated with some surrounding fluid and soft tissue stranding.
Image 2: An axial contrast-enhanced CT scan of the upper abdomen. The image shows the liver, kidneys, and bowel loops. In the anterior midline, there is a thick-walled, heterogeneous, low-attenuation mass with internal nodular areas of enhancement. A letter 'B' is visible in the upper right corner of the image.
Image 3: A gross pathology photograph shows a surgical specimen of a uterus and cervix. The organ is held by a metal surgical retractor. The uterine wall is open, revealing a large, irregular, dark red to purple hemorrhagic mass within the endometrial cavity. The surrounding tissue is erythematous and blood-stained, and the specimen is positioned within a surgical field draped in blue.

Demographics: 58-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Recurrent fever episodes with fatigue and elevated infection markers
History of Present Illness: After recovery from left ventricular assist device implantation, the patient began experiencing recurrent fevers, marked fatigue, and laboratory evidence of kidney retention. No clear infectious focus was identified, and he was initially treated empirically with ampicillin/sulbactam, then switched to ciprofloxacin and later fosfomycin without improvement. PET-CT performed at a referring center revealed an anterior intrapericardial inflammatory process involving the LVAD outflow graft and portions of the pacemaker lead. He was transferred to our institution, where subsequent blood cultures grew a gram-positive organism, prompting a change to flucloxacillin. During this therapy the patient developed a new fever (38.9 °C), mental confusion, and visual disturbances described as “dots and stars.” Neurological examination showed left homonymous hemianopsia. Initial non-contrast cerebral CT demonstrated scattered atypical hemorrhagic foci in both hemispheres and extra-axial blood collections on the left side. Follow-up contrast CT identified two hypodense parietal-occipital lesions with scalloped microvascular appearances and a 2.5 cm hyperdense ring-like enhancement surrounded by edema. Serial imaging over the ensuing weeks showed progressive reduction in lesion size and surrounding edema.
Past Medical History: End-stage heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy; Left ventricular assist device implantation (bridge-to-transplant); Permanent pacemaker
Exposures/Risk Factors: LVAD device; Pacemaker lead; Prior courses of ampicillin/sulbactam, ciprofloxacin, fosfomycin; Hospitalization with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Physical Exam Findings: Confusion/altered mental status; Left homonymous hemianopsia; No other focal neurological deficits
Lab Findings: Temperature 38.9 °C (102 °F) during later episode; Elevated infection parameters (unspecified); Evidence of renal retention (elevated creatinine)
Imaging Findings: PET-CT: anterior intrapericardial inflammation involving LVAD outflow graft and caudal portion of pacemaker lead; Cerebral CT (initial): scattered atypical hemorrhagic foci in both hemispheres and extra-axial blood collections left hemisphere, unchanged on repeat after six hours; Contrast cerebral CT (subsequent): two hypodense parietal and occipital areas with scalloped microvascular appearances, hyperdense 2.5 cm ring-like enhancement with surrounding edema; Follow-up contrast CT after one week: slight reduction in lesion dimensions (approximately 19 × 18 × 20 mm) and decreased perilesional edema; Contrast CT after seven weeks: marked reduction of lesions and perifocal edema; Contrast CT after thirteen weeks: near-complete resolution of lesions
Image Findings:
Image 1: Three axial non-contrast CT images of the head at the level of the upper cerebral hemispheres. The images show prominent cerebral sulci and enlarged ventricles, consistent with generalized cortical atrophy. No focal masses, midline shift, or acute intracranial hemorrhages are visible. There are no annotations or labels present in the images.

Demographics: 71-year-old male
Chief Complaint: persistent abdominal pain
History of Present Illness: One month after his seventh treatment, the patient experienced persistent abdominal pain accompanied by intermittent fever, chills, and weight loss. Initial abdominal CT demonstrated a gas-containing cavity within a necrotic hepatic mass in the left lateral segment. He was hospitalized, received intravenous antibiotics, and underwent ultrasound-guided aspiration, which yielded turbid yellowish fluid with foul odor; cultures grew anaerobic bacteria. After two weeks of antibiotics his symptoms resolved and he was discharged on oral antibiotics. Two weeks after discharge the abdominal pain recurred and gradually worsened, prompting readmission. Physical examination revealed right upper quadrant tenderness and a rise in serum C-reactive protein compared with the prior admission. Follow-up CT showed a reduction in the size of the cavity but revealed a new communication between the remaining cavity and the duodenal bulb. Endoscopic evaluation confirmed a small (approximately 0.3 cm) opening in the proximal duodenal bulb, which was initially clipped. Persistent opening was noted on repeat endoscopy; subsequently, a guidewire was used to access the tract and a mixture of cyanoacrylate glue and contrast was injected, achieving closure of the opening. The patient tolerated oral intake without pain and was discharged. Subsequent imaging at one month demonstrated obliteration of the tract and further decrease of the cavity, and later scans showed progression of the underlying liver mass without recurrence of the cavity or communication.
Past Medical History: chronic hepatitis B infection; history of malignant liver tumor with vascular invasion; previous portal vein thrombosis
Physical Exam Findings: right upper quadrant tenderness
Lab Findings: elevated serum C-reactive protein level compared with previous hospitalization
Imaging Findings: CT: gas-containing cavity within necrotic hepatic mass in left lateral segment of liver; CT follow-up: decreased size of cavity; CT follow-up: new communication between residual cavity and duodenal bulb; CT at one month post-intervention: obliteration of communication tract and further reduction of cavity; CT later: progression of liver mass without cavity or communication
Image Findings:
Image 1: A coronal CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis. The image shows the liver in the right upper quadrant and loops of bowel throughout the central and lower abdomen. There is a prominent, air-filled loop of bowel in the mid-abdomen with thickened, irregular walls and a scalloped internal border. No annotations are present in the image.
Image 2: A coronal CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis shows a thickened, loop-like structure in the upper abdomen. Three white arrows point to the wall of this structure, which exhibits concentric layers of varying density. The surrounding abdominal cavity contains multiple air-filled bowel loops and soft tissue structures. A label 'B' is located in the bottom left corner, and a label '[H]' is visible at the top center of the image.
Image 3: A coronal CT scan of the abdomen and lower chest. The image shows the liver, gallbladder, and bowel loops. In the upper central abdomen, there is a low-attenuation, fluid-filled collection adjacent to the pancreas and stomach. The stomach contains mottled gas and debris. A white label with the letter "C" is located in the bottom-left corner, and a label "[H]" is visible in the upper central region over the heart.
Image 4: An endoscopic image of a mucosal surface, likely from the gastrointestinal tract. The mucosa is predominantly pinkish-red with a visible linear red streak and a small, dark, circular opening or pit in the lower left quadrant. A white label "A" is located in the bottom left corner of the image.
Image 5: An endoscopic image showing a view of a tubular anatomical lumen with reddish-pink mucosal lining. A metallic instrument and a blue-tipped probe are visible in the upper right quadrant, extending into the lumen. A white square label containing the letter "B" is located in the bottom left corner. Text is partially visible in the upper right corner, including the phrase "Study Time: 09".
Image 6: An endoscopic image of a mucosal surface showing areas of erythema and focal red patches. A small amount of yellowish-green fluid is visible in the lower left quadrant, and there are bright white specular reflections from the light source. A white square containing the letter "C" is located in the bottom left corner, and partial text is visible in the top right corner.

Demographics: 22-year-old female
Chief Complaint: trouble with mandibular left first molar
History of Present Illness: The patient reported persistent discomfort with the mandibular left first molar despite an initial root canal treatment that was deemed unsuccessful. She subsequently underwent nonsurgical retreatment by an endodontist, but the discomfort continued. She denied any soft-tissue swelling, abscess formation, or sinus tract associated with the tooth. The tooth had a composite resin restoration. No other medical issues were reported.
Physical Exam Findings: Normal mucosa in the adjacent vestibule; Tooth tender to percussion; Normal probing depth; No tooth mobility
Lab Findings: Histopathology demonstrated a sulfur granule containing gram-positive branching filamentous organisms
Imaging Findings: Radiograph showed previously performed root canal therapy of good quality; Large radiolucent area surrounding the mesial root; Small radiolucent area at the apex of the distal root; Post-operative periapical radiograph confirmed precise repositioning of the replanted tooth; Follow-up radiograph at two months showed marked bone healing
Image Findings:
Image 1: This figure consists of two histopathology images stained with hematoxylin and eosin. The main image is a higher-magnification view showing a dense, basophilic, nodular collection of cells embedded within a lighter pink, eosinophilic background of tissue. An inset image provides a lower-magnification view of a circular tissue section, showing a similar basophilic nodular region located eccentrically within a larger, pale pink circular area, which is surrounded by a darker purple peripheral rim.

Demographics: 40-year-old female
Chief Complaint: severe abdominal pain for three months and a gradually increasing abdominal mass for 15 days
History of Present Illness: The patient experienced progressively worsening abdominal pain over three months, accompanied by low-grade fever and a 2 kg weight loss. About two weeks before admission, she noted a palpable abdominal mass that was increasing in size. She had a long-standing intrauterine contraceptive device in place for 21 years, which was removed in April 2020 due to pain escalation. She sought hospital care in May 2020 because of the worsening pain and enlarging mass.
Past Medical History: pulmonary tuberculosis in 2003 (completed 9-month anti-tuberculosis therapy); intrauterine contraceptive device retained for 21 years, removed April 2020
Exposures/Risk Factors: long-term intrauterine device retention; history of prior pulmonary tuberculosis
Physical Exam Findings: ill-looking appearance; mild pallor; tenderness on superficial and deep palpation of lower abdomen; ill-defined 6 cm × 7 cm mass located 1 cm lateral to umbilicus; mass tender, irreducible, mobile, firm; negative cough impulse; negative Carnett sign; digital rectal exam unremarkable
Lab Findings: WBC 14.2 × 10⁹/L; Neutrophils 85.9 % of leukocytes; Hemoglobin 8.4 g/L; C-reactive protein within normal range; Blood cultures negative; Urine cultures negative; HIV screening negative; TB acid-fast bacilli staining of sputum negative; Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR negative; Other laboratory parameters within normal limits
Imaging Findings: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast showing heterogeneous enhancement of soft tissue in left anterior abdominal wall involving left rectus abdominis muscle at umbilicus level, measuring approximately 5.1 cm × 2.6 cm; associated fat stranding separate from anterior surface of transverse colon; mild circumferential mural thickening of distal one-third of transverse colon with pericolonic fat stranding; multiple prominent pericolonic lymph nodes, largest 1.1 cm × 0.7 cm; colonoscopy unremarkable

Demographics: 29-year-old male
Chief Complaint: intermittent pus discharge from the lower jaw where Tooth 47 was extracted five years ago
History of Present Illness: The patient reports that ever since the extraction of Tooth 47 about five years ago, he has experienced intermittent suppuration from the same area. He has taken several courses of oral antibiotics—including amoxicillin, clindamycin, and azithromycin—over the years without lasting improvement. No microbiological cultures were performed during previous visits. The problem persisted, leading to referral for further evaluation.
Exposures/Risk Factors: extraction of Tooth 47 five years ago; multiple courses of oral antibiotics (amoxicillin, clindamycin, azithromycin)
Physical Exam Findings: intraoral fistula/sinus tract in the region of the extracted Tooth 47; no redness of the overlying mucous membrane; purulent exudate expressed on slight pressure to the gingiva; mild tenderness on palpation; no cervical lymphadenopathy
Lab Findings: histopathology: necrotic bone trabeculae with partially resorbed sequestra; presence of yellowish granules containing radiating basophilic filaments and eosinophilic club-shaped ends; granulation tissue with vascular proliferation and polymorphonuclear inflammatory cells
Imaging Findings: segmental radiograph of the mandible showing ill-defined bony changes with mixed osteolytic and osteosclerotic areas

Demographics: 56-year-old female
Chief Complaint: low back pain radiating to both buttocks with burning sensations in the lower limbs, claudication distance <100 m, weakness in both feet and difficulty putting on footwear
History of Present Illness: The patient presented with several months of severe low back pain (VAS 7) radiating to the buttocks and legs (leg VAS 8), associated with burning sensations, limited walking distance (<100 m), and progressive weakness in the feet. She reported constitutional symptoms of weight loss and loss of appetite. Conservative treatments at multiple hospitals provided no relief. Neurological examination showed bilateral positive straight leg raise at 30°, grade 3 weakness of toe and ankle dorsiflexors, and ~50% reduced sensation in the L4–L5 dermatomes. Imaging revealed extensive vertebral and sacral marrow edema with soft-tissue extension. She underwent posterior laminectomy and decompression with tissue biopsy; histopathology did not show malignancy. Post-operative pain and mobility improved (VAS reduced to 4). Three months later she returned with recurrent burning leg sensations, inability to stand/walk for long periods, and discharging sinuses over the back. Repeat imaging demonstrated new patchy marrow signal abnormalities, ring-enhancing lesions in lumbar vertebrae, and additional involvement of paraspinal muscles and right ilium. Laboratory inflammatory markers were rising. She underwent revision decompression with removal of thick epidural granulation tissue. Subsequent follow-up showed gradual clinical improvement with decreasing pain scores and radiographic resolution of osteopenia and marrow abnormalities over the next six months.

Demographics: 34-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Sudden colic-like, persistent anterior chest pain
History of Present Illness: The patient experienced sudden onset of persistent anterior chest pain described as colic-like. Within about 50 minutes he presented to the emergency department where an electrocardiogram showed sinus arrest with a junctional rhythm, ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF and ST-segment depression in leads I, aVL, V1-V6. Cardiac biomarkers were markedly elevated (troponin I 27.052 ng/ml, myoglobin 4,102 ng/ml, CK-MB 297 U/L). Emergent coronary angiography demonstrated no obstructive disease in the left main, left anterior descending, or left circumflex arteries, but the right coronary artery could not be engaged due to an abnormal origin between the non-coronary and left coronary sinuses. During the procedure the patient suffered recurrent life-threatening arrhythmias requiring electrical cardioversion and defibrillation. He required pharmacologic rate control, vasopressor support, intra-aortic balloon pump, endotracheal intubation, ventilatory support, and venous-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. He was then transferred for further care. Subsequent echocardiography showed severely reduced left ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 26%, and serology was positive for coxsackie B IgM. Over the following days he developed multi-organ impairment involving circulatory, respiratory, renal, and hepatic systems, necessitating continuous renal replacement therapy and corticosteroid therapy. Gradual clinical improvement allowed weaning from mechanical support and eventual discharge after 27 days.

Demographics: 36-year-old

Following the acute illness, they reported markedly reduced physical resilience and persistent fatigue, with a Bell score of 20 and sleep duration increasing to 12-14 hours per day. Approximately 1.5 years after symptom onset, a trial of 5 mg amifampridine was initiated, resulting within one day in notable improvement of fatigue and muscle complaints, increase of the Bell score to 50, and reduction of sleep time to 8-10 hours per day. The beneficial effects on exercise tolerance and sleep were reproducible with intermittent dosing. Ongoing limitation of exercise capacity was attributed to cardiac-related concerns, and after cardiac rehabilitation a return to work was planned.

Demographics: 73-year-old male
Chief Complaint: difficulty breathing
History of Present Illness: The patient had a history of chronic respiratory problems and had been receiving long-term steroids and tacrolimus, along with prophylactic sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. Two months earlier he had been treated with oral amphotericin B for oral fungal infection. On admission his C-reactive protein was normal (0.24 mg/dL) but his white blood cell count was elevated (12.6 ×10^9/L) with marked neutrophilia (94.4%). He was hospitalized for a presumed flare of his chronic lung condition and received continued immunosuppression, antihyperglycaemic therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation and supportive care. Respiratory status improved by hospital day 40, when he suddenly developed acute abdominal pain. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated free intra-abdominal air and fecal material. Blood cultures were drawn; one anaerobic bottle grew Gram-positive cocci after 30.5 h. He underwent emergency laparotomy, which revealed a defect in the sigmoid colon with leakage of stool and food residue; a colostomy, drainage and irrigation were performed. Post-operatively he required ICU care with fluids, vasopressors, mechanical ventilation and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Subsequent cultures of peritoneal fluid grew Escherichia coli (an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producer), Enterococcus avium and Enterococcus faecalis. The wound later demonstrated growth of the same organisms, prompting additional antibiotic therapy. An elevated plasma (1→3)-β-D-glucan level led to initiation of intravenous micafungin. Several weeks later he experienced watery diarrhoea; a toxin-producing Clostridioides strain was identified by a nucleic-acid assay, and treatment with oral metronidazole followed by treatment was given. Later he again developed fever and a rise in C-reactive protein, which responded to a short course of meropenem. He was discharged after a five-month hospital stay.

Exposures/Risk Factors: immunosuppressive therapy with prednisolone and tacrolimus; prophylactic sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim; prior oral amphotericin B therapy; hospitalization with multiple invasive procedures; broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure

Demographics: 59-year-old female
Chief Complaint: I have been feeling very tired, have fever, and have been producing very little urine.
History of Present Illness: Six days after onset of fatigue, fever, and decreased urine output, the patient was admitted. Initial chest radiograph showed infiltrates. Because of elevated serum creatinine, a monoclonal antibody therapy was given instead of an antiviral medication. The next day, low-flow oxygen and a short course of intravenous steroids were started. Renal function worsened, with serum creatinine rising to over 7 mg/dL and BUN above 120 mg/dL, prompting transfer to a tertiary center on day 12. On arrival she was afebrile but tachypneic, with late inspiratory crackles in the lower lung fields. Metabolic acidosis with low bicarbonate was noted on arterial blood gas. Laboratory studies confirmed ongoing renal dysfunction, mild inflammatory marker elevation, and an elevated D-dimer. Urine analysis showed pyuria and gram-negative rods, consistent with prior recurrent infections, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics were initiated. After rehydration, renal function improved. Two days after transfer the patient developed dyspnea and desaturation while seated, requiring high-flow oxygen. Computed tomography demonstrated worsening bilateral peripheral and patchy ground-glass opacities. Intravenous steroids were increased, and the antimetabolite immunosuppressant was held. On day 18, oxygen saturation was markedly lower in the upright position compared with supine. An elevated D-dimer and contrast-enhanced CT identified a pulmonary artery defect in the right upper lobe; anticoagulation was started. Positional desaturation persisted even with mild symptoms. Serial arterial blood gases in supine and seated positions confirmed lower oxygen tensions when upright. Over the following weeks, steroid dosing was tapered, pulmonary opacities decreased, and the pulmonary artery defect resolved. By day 47 the SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative, dyspnea resolved, oxygen was weaned, and positional desaturation improved. The patient was discharged home on day 56.

Demographics: 90-year-old male
Chief Complaint: difficulty swallowing with frequent choking and coughing
History of Present Illness: The patient experienced an acute brain lesion in the left medial temporal lobe on January 2, 2022, resulting in right-sided weakness and inability to walk independently. He was admitted for post-event rehabilitation 3.5 months later (March 16, 2022). At that time he was bedridden due to right hemiplegia, fed via nasogastric tube (FOIS 1), and demonstrated reduced tongue motion, weak cough, mild facial weakness, and a delayed swallowing reflex. Over the next weeks fiberoptic endoscopic and videofluoroscopic evaluations showed delayed reflexes, premature leakage, and minimal aspiration of thin liquids, leading to removal of the tube on April 1, 2022 and transition to a modified diet (FOIS 5). Two months after discharge (June 19, 2022) he developed fever, cough, and rhinorrhea due to a viral respiratory infection; oral antiviral therapy and brief supplemental oxygen were provided, and symptoms resolved by June 22. One week later he required reinsertion of the nasogastric tube because of frequent choking and coughing on saliva or small sips of water. By three weeks post-infection his upper respiratory symptoms had cleared, but swallowing problems persisted, and he was readmitted for swallowing training on August 2, 2022. On this admission he had good orientation, persistent right-side weakness, weakened trunk muscles, drooling, wet voice, markedly delayed swallowing reflex, and diminished gag reflexes bilaterally. Brain MRI showed no new lesions. Videofluoroscopic study on August 8, 2022 revealed severe swallowing difficulty with premature leakage, delayed reflex, inadequate hypopharyngeal elevation, large bolus retention, and aspiration of both thin and thick liquids. He then underwent neurostimulation-based swallowing therapy (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and neuromuscular electrical stimulation) combined with traditional swallowing exercises. Over the ensuing weeks his oral motor control, cough strength, and laryngeal elevation improved, allowing gradual advancement of oral intake. He was readmitted on September 22, 2022 for a trial of tube removal; subsequent videofluoroscopic study on October 7, 2022 showed improved bolus transit, reduced leakage, limited aspiration, and minimal residue. The nasogastric tube was removed on October 7, 2022. At follow-up one month later he was clinically stable, had gained weight, and showed no signs of lung infection.

Demographics: 51-year-old Chinese female

Upper and lower endoscopies revealed multiple superficial lesions in the duodenum and active oozing of blood from the ileocecal region. Biopsies showed lymphocytic duodenitis. Because bleeding could not be controlled medically, selective arterial embolization of a branch of the pancreaticoduodenal artery was performed using gelatin sponge particles, resulting in cessation of bleeding and gradual improvement in blood counts.

At 34 weeks a repeat ultrasound and fetal MRI showed enlargement of the lateral ventricles (left atrial diameter 12.4 mm, right 13 mm). The infant was delivered by cesarean section at 35 weeks due to fetal distress. Within the first hour after birth a cranial ultrasound demonstrated mild ventricular enlargement and a small intracranial bleed. Four hours later diffuse petechiae appeared over the body. Laboratory testing revealed a positive IgM serology and a positive polymerase chain reaction for viral DNA in the blood. The infant remained without respiratory distress; chest X-ray were initially normal. On day 20, abdominal distension and feeding intolerance prompted imaging that identified a regular-shaped air-filled lesion in the left lower lung zone, confirmed on thoracic CT as multiple air-containing areas in that lobe. C-reactive protein was normal and blood cultures were negative. Subsequent imaging at day 35 showed resolution of the lung lesions. Follow-up ophthalmologic examination later demonstrated macular scarring, and auditory testing indicated profound hearing impairment. At six months, growth parameters were within normal percentiles, and cranial MRI revealed bilateral periventricular fluid-filled spaces.
Exposures/Risk Factors: Maternal serology negative for rubella, toxoplasma, and cytomegalovirus IgM; Normal fetal karyotype on amniocentesis; Prematurity (35 weeks)
Physical Exam Findings: Well-appearing newborn; Diffuse petechiae over entire body
Lab Findings: C-reactive protein within normal limits; Blood cultures negative

Demographics: 70-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Worsening vision in the right eye
History of Present Illness: The patient had previously undergone cataract extraction in both eyes with intraocular lens implantation. Postoperatively the right eye visual acuity was 6/12, but three months later it decreased to 6/36 and the cornea became edematous with hazy appearance, epithelial swelling, descemet membrane striae, and pigmented keratic precipitates. He subsequently underwent Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK) in the right eye. After surgery he developed elevated intraocular pressure attributed to steroid use and required trabeculectomy with mitomycin C. Within a week the right eye visual acuity further declined to 4/60 due to early graft rejection. He received intravenous methylprednisolone for three days followed by topical dexamethasone and oral prednisolone with tapering. Vision continued to worsen to 1/60, prompting repeat DSAEK for graft failure. A second course of intravenous methylprednisolone was administered and antiviral therapy was started. Over the next two weeks visual acuity improved to 2/60 and the keratic precipitates decreased. A repeat anterior chamber tap is planned in six months with consideration of further surgical intervention.
Past Medical History: Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy (bilateral); Bilaterally pseudophakic following cataract surgery; Prior right eye cataract extraction complicated by posterior capsule rupture
Exposures/Risk Factors: Multiple ocular surgeries (cataract extraction, endothelial keratoplasty, trabeculectomy); Systemic and topical corticosteroid therapy

Demographics: 46-year-old male

History of Present Illness: The patient had previously been hospitalized for dyspnea and fatigue related to severe aortic valve stenosis and underwent surgical aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. He recovered uneventfully and was discharged home. Approximately one month after discharge, he developed a high-grade fever and chills lasting a few days, followed by sudden onset chest pain, dyspnea, and vomiting. He presented to the emergency department appearing lethargic, pale, and hemodynamically unstable with cold extremities and weak pulses. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy and ST-segment depression in posterior and lateral leads. Cardiac enzymes were markedly elevated. An emergent coronary angiogram demonstrated a long, complex lesion of the left main coronary artery with about 80% lumen narrowing and tapering suggestive of external compression. Blood cultures later grew oxacillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed mobile masses attached to the prosthetic valve, a localized collection in the aortic root region, and evidence of flow between the aortic root area and the right atrium. Chest computed tomography suggested that the left main coronary compression was due to the aortic root collection or surrounding hematoma. The patient required intra-aortic balloon pump support, intravenous fluids, inotropes, mechanical ventilation, and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy. He subsequently underwent re-operative aortic root reconstruction with homograft replacement, closure of the communication with a pericardial patch, and coronary artery bypass grafting to the left anterior descending artery. Post-operatively he experienced acute renal insufficiency requiring dialysis, transient hepatic dysfunction, prolonged ventilation, and required permanent pacemaker implantation. Over the following weeks his ventricular function improved and he was discharged home in good condition.

Demographics: 68-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Shortness of breath, fatigue and low blood counts
History of Present Illness: The patient first presented with neutropenia, dyspnea and tiredness. Laboratory testing showed leukopenia with a white blood cell count of 7.81 × 10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count of 0.09 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin of 68 g/L and platelets of 77 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow examination revealed a hypercellular marrow with 92% blasts. He received a 7-day course of treatment as a bridging therapy and was started on supportive antibiotics (levofloxacin). He was discharged after the pulmonary infection was controlled.

One month later he was readmitted for the next chemotherapy cycle. At that time labs showed WBC 20.58 × 10^9/L, ANC 0.69 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 28 g/L, platelets 99 × 10^9/L and bone marrow blasts 72%. He again developed fever and was treated with levofloxacin and tigecycline, followed by a 7-day treatment regimen and a 28-day course of treatment. Four days after chemotherapy he experienced worsening breathlessness, cough, fever (up to 39.2 °C) and developed profound neutropenia (nadir WBC 0.19 × 10^9/L, ANC 0.04 × 10^9/L) and thrombocytopenia (nadir platelets 12 × 10^9/L). Repeated cultures and serum fungal antigen tests (galactomannan, 1,3-β-D-glucan) were negative. Empirical broad-spectrum antibacterial agents (including carbapenems, beta-lactams and colistimethate) and antifungal agents (caspofungin, posaconazole, voriconazole) were administered without clinical improvement. Auscultation revealed progressive loss of breath sounds over the right lung. Chest CT showed progression of the pulmonary infiltrates.

Due to improving platelet counts (199 × 10^9/L), bronchoscopy was performed and revealed an endobronchial obstructing mass in the right main bronchus. Antifungal therapy with treatment cholesteryl sulfate complex was initiated, leading to rapid defervescence. Nebulized treatment was added subsequently. Over the following weeks his blood counts recovered, peripheral blasts cleared, and imaging showed stabilization of the lung lesions. He was discharged on oral posaconazole. Seven days after discharge he experienced a sudden violent cough with expectoration of dark red necrotic material and died suddenly at home.

Demographics: 61-year-old female
Chief Complaint: fever and headache
History of Present Illness: The patient, a 61-year-old woman with an eight-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and poor glycaemic control, presented with fever, headache, severe loss of appetite, lethargy and apathy. On examination she was dehydrated, appeared very ill, and had an erythematous, tender patch over the right maxillary bone. Laboratory tests showed marked neutrophilic leukocytosis and a C-reactive protein level above 200 mg/L. An occipito-mental x-ray demonstrated an opacity in the right maxillary sinus. Initial intravenous ceftriaxone therapy was started, but her condition worsened with a drop in blood pressure, necessitating intensive-care support, fluid resuscitation and vasopressor therapy. Intravenous meropenem was later administered. Over the next days the overlying skin over the right maxillary bone became necrotic, prompting antifungal treatment. Imaging revealed a fluid collection in the left psoas region, which was aspirated under ultrasound guidance on two occasions and later surgically drained. Despite therapy, the bone of the maxillary sinus continued to erode, extending toward the orbital area, leading to an increase in antifungal dosage. Two weeks after a repeat rhinoscopic washout, the patient’s level of consciousness abruptly declined; metabolic screening was normal. Non-contrast head CT showed the presence of air within the cerebral parenchyma, lateral ventricles and around the pituitary stalk. High-flow oxygen was provided, resulting in gradual neurological improvement and radiologic resolution of the intracranial air over the subsequent week. The patient eventually recovered clinically and was referred for facial reconstructive surgery.

Exposures/Risk Factors: residence in Batticaloa District, Sri Lanka; poorly controlled diabetes mellitus

He then developed a very low heart rate of 40 beats/min that did not respond to atropine. Therapeutic treatment with albumin replacement was started every two days. After the first exchange his heart rate improved (>55 beats/min). Respiratory support was weaned over five days, and neurological function gradually recovered, returning to baseline by three months after discharge.

Demographics: 38-year-old male
Chief Complaint: fatigue, loss of appetite, yellowing of the skin and eyes, intense itching, and unintended weight loss of about 7 kg
History of Present Illness: In June 2019 the patient developed fatigue, anorexia, jaundice, pruritus and lost about 7 kg. Initial laboratory testing showed markedly elevated bilirubin and transaminases. Abdominal CT demonstrated a nodular liver appearance, splenomegaly and variceal formation. Three days after admission he experienced hematochezia, which was managed with hemostatic agents. Fifteen days later a diffuse maculopapular rash appeared on the trunk, accompanied by fever up to 39 °C, prompting transfer to a tertiary hospital. On admission he was lethargic with hypotension, severe jaundice, icteric sclera and a maculopapular rash on the trunk. Laboratory studies showed leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, modestly elevated transaminases, very high bilirubin, prolonged prothrombin time, low albumin and total protein. Over the next week the rash spread to the upper arms, axillae, palms, soles and became more congestive. He was started on systemic corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin. By day 12 the rash progressed with a positive Nikolsky sign, blister formation on hands, feet, lips and later on limbs, shoulders, neck, buttocks and back, ulceration of oral mucosa, difficulty opening the mouth, and ulceration of external genitalia. Skin detachment involved approximately 30 % of body surface area. On day 15 bilateral eye redness, edema and conjunctival congestion were noted. Despite escalated corticosteroid therapy and continued immunoglobulin, the skin lesions gradually stabilized. By late July the cutaneous and mucosal lesions largely resolved and ocular findings improved. On 16 August the patient developed fever, cough and dyspnea; laboratory evaluation showed a normal white blood cell count, mildly elevated C-reactive protein and CD4+ T-cell count below 200 cells/µL. Chest CT revealed ground-glass and septal reticular changes. Empiric therapy for a presumed opportunistic pulmonary infection was initiated, leading to clinical and radiologic improvement. The patient was discharged in early September with stable organ function and complete resolution of skin lesions.

Demographics: 26-year-old male
Chief Complaint: persistent stabbing pain in the waist and back
History of Present Illness: Three months prior, routine examination revealed severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 29 × 10⁹/L) with occasional gingival bleeding. Four days later, hematology evaluation showed pancytopenia (Hb 9.8 g/dL, reticulocytes 3.5 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 2.2 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 1.0 × 10⁹/L, platelets 30 × 10⁹/L) and bone-marrow aspiration demonstrated marked hypoplasia (~25% cellularity) with occasional megakaryocytes. Flow cytometry identified a clone of interest, and treatment with hormones, cyclosporine and traditional Chinese medicine was initiated, with stable laboratory parameters on follow-up. On 26 November, the patient presented with a 2-day history of stabbing waist and back pain, abdominal discomfort, edema of the limbs, and erythematous swelling with pruritus of the glans and prepuce. Laboratory tests showed mild worsening of cytopenias (Hb 11.5 g/dL, leukocytes 2.7 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 1.8 × 10⁹/L, platelets 14 × 10⁹/L) and slight elevations of liver enzymes. Imaging identified fatty liver. Three days later, he developed high fever (38.9 °C) and persistent abdominal pain; CT scan revealed fatty liver, gas accumulation and colonic distension. The next day he became unconscious, hypotensive (90/40 mmHg), bradycardic (39 bpm) and tachypneic, then suffered cardiac arrest requiring resuscitation. Post-resuscitation, he remained comatose on ventilatory support, with diffuse skin lesions ranging from vesicles to crusted pustules. Laboratory studies demonstrated severe anemia (Hb 1.6 g/dL), leukopenia (0.8 × 10⁹/L), neutropenia (0.6 × 10⁹/L), thrombocytopenia (9 × 10⁹/L), markedly elevated transaminases (AST 7360 U/L, ALT 9780 U/L), increased direct bilirubin (13.6 µmol/L), high serum creatinine (240.2 µmol/L), elevated D-dimer (>80 000 µg/L), positive plasma protamine paracoagulation test, and raised cardiac troponin I (1.78 ng/mL). Despite broad-spectrum anti-infection therapy, blood product transfusion, and intensive life-support measures, the patient died eight hours later.

Demographics: 69-year-old woman

History of Present Illness: The patient was admitted at night because of acute upper abdominal pain. She has a history of hypertension. Initial CT scan demonstrated an enlarged gallbladder with a thickened, enhancing wall and an intraluminal stone, without surrounding fluid collection. The patient subsequently underwent organ removal and drainage procedures, recovered without complications, and was discharged on postoperative day 9.

Demographics: 65-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Decreased urine output, fever, and abdominal pain over the past week
History of Present Illness: The patient underwent cystoscopy, bilateral double-J (DJ) ureteral stent placement, and urethrotomy for a urethral stricture with severe bilateral hydronephrosis at an outside facility. During this period his urine output further declined and he developed fever and worsening abdominal discomfort. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen, as well as marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia. Imaging demonstrated migration of the right stent upward and the left stent displaced into the abdominal cavity with suspected involvement of the bladder and a segment of small intestine, together with moderate free intra-abdominal fluid. He required urgent hemodialysis and broad-spectrum antibiotics. After stabilization, the right stent was removed endoscopically, while the left stent could not be accessed via the ureteral orifice due to multiple false passages and bladder mucosal trauma. Open surgical exploration revealed that the left stent had traversed the bladder wall and a loop of small intestine, causing adhesion between the bladder and bowel, and an injury to the bladder wall. The injured bowel segment was resected and an anastomosis performed; the bladder defect was repaired, and a drain placed.

History of Present Illness: The patient experienced an abrupt development of left-eye discharge and ocular pain. On examination, a corneal ulceration with opacity was observed, together with conjunctival redness and swelling. Topical and oral antibiotics were started, and bacterial cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus canis, both sensitive to the prescribed fluoroquinolone. After two weeks, the infection resolved but a small (≈1 mm) corneal epithelial defect remained despite intensified lubrication. The defect persisted for another two weeks until it healed with additional topical therapy. Approximately two months after the initial presentation, intra-ocular bleeding into the vitreous cavity was noted, accompanied by a decline in visual acuity, leading to vitrectomy after the epithelial defect closed. Post-surgery, the ocular surface remained stable and visual acuity improved.
Past Medical History: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (35 years); Bilateral cataract surgery (~20 years ago); Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (~23 years, no prior retinal photocoagulation)
Exposures/Risk Factors: Chronic hyperglycemia (HbA1c 7.2-8.0 % historically, 7.3 % at presentation); Prior ocular surgeries
Physical Exam Findings: Left corneal ulceration with opacity; Conjunctival injection; Chemosis and lower bulbar conjunctival redundancy; Mild retinal punctate hemorrhages in both eyes on fundus exam; Corrected visual acuity 14/20 (right) and 16/20 (left) initially; Schirmer test: 12 mm (right), 11 mm (left); Tear break-up time: 4 seconds in both eyes; Non-healing corneal epithelial defect ~1 mm size persisting after infection control; Intra-ocular vitreous bleeding observed in left eye with decreased visual acuity
Lab Findings: Blood HbA1c 7.3%; Corneal scrapings culture positive for Staphylococcus aureus (sensitive to levofloxacin); Corneal scrapings culture positive for Streptococcus canis (sensitive to levofloxacin)
Imaging Findings: Fundus examination showing mild retinal punctate hemorrhages in both eyes

Demographics: 67-year-old female
Chief Complaint: Accidental injury to the right eye from a falling chestnut
History of Present Illness: The patient sustained a mechanical injury to the right eye when a chestnut fell onto it. She initially received topical ofloxacin ointment at a local eye clinic. The following day, worsening ocular findings prompted referral to the hospital. On presentation she reported mild pain. Visual acuity was 0.8 in the right eye and 1.5 in the left eye. Examination revealed a central corneal wound with aqueous leakage (positive Seidel test) despite a deep anterior chamber. There was conjunctival injection, corneal cell infiltration surrounding the wound, moderate anterior chamber cells, iris damage, and pigment opacification of the anterior lens capsule. The corneal thickness measured 603 µm. Early cataract and pterygium were noted. No foreign bodies were identified. Over the subsequent days the Seidel test became negative, a soft hydroxyethyl methacrylate contact lens was placed briefly, then removed. Cell infiltration persisted with fluctuating anterior chamber reaction. Descemet membrane folds appeared on day 3. By day 9 cultures grew Propionibacterium acnes, fungi were not detected, and antibiotic therapy was continued. Gradual improvement in visual acuity, reduction of anterior chamber reaction, and healing of the corneal wound were observed through day 26, with final BCVA of 1.0 in the right eye.
Exposures/Risk Factors: Accidental ocular trauma from falling chestnut; Topical ofloxacin ointment use; Placement of soft hydroxyethyl methacrylate contact lens
Physical Exam Findings: Best-corrected visual acuity: 0.8 (right eye), 1.5 (left eye); Central corneal wound with aqueous leakage (positive Seidel test); Deep anterior chamber; Conjunctival injection; Corneal cell infiltration around wound; Moderate cells in anterior chamber; Iris damage; Anterior lens capsule opacified with pigments; Corneal thickness 603 µm; Slight cataract; Early pterygium; No foreign body detected in conjunctival sac, cornea, or anterior chamber; Gonioscopic exam: no hemorrhage or foreign body at angle; Fundus: no abnormality
Lab Findings: Corneal scrapings: gram-positive cocci, few neutrophils; Culture: Propionibacterium acnes, sensitive to levofloxacin and cefmenoxime; Fungal elements: not detected; Corneal endothelial cell density: 2,778 cells/mm² (right eye), 2,793 cells/mm² (left eye)
Imaging Findings: Anterior segment OCT: corneal wound involving endothelial layer; central thickness 603 µm (initial); Anterior segment OCT: appearance of inner wound closure (day 3); Anterior segment OCT: healing of corneal wound with thickness reduced to 523 µm (day 26); Corneal shape analysis: no irregular astigmatism observed

Demographics: 23-year-old male
Chief Complaint: pain and redness in the left eye
History of Present Illness: The patient underwent SMILE refractive surgery on both eyes. On postoperative day 1 his uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA) was 20/20 bilaterally. On postoperative day 3 he noticed pain and redness in the left eye and his UCVA declined to 20/50, prompting referral. Slit-lamp examination showed a paracentral, white, cross-shaped infiltrate at the corneal cap-stromal bed interface. Initial empirical topical antibiotics did not improve the findings, and corneal cap melting was observed. The infiltrate was scraped for smear and culture; the smear showed Gram-positive cocci while cultures remained negative, likely due to prior topical antibiotics. Intensive topical antibiotic therapy was continued, followed by tapering and addition of a corticosteroid. By two weeks the infiltrate had regressed, and at one month the UCVA returned to 20/20 with only a trace peripheral scar.
Exposures/Risk Factors: SMILE refractive surgery; post-operative prophylactic topical antibiotics
Physical Exam Findings: UCVA 20/20 in both eyes on postoperative day 1; UCVA 20/50 in left eye on postoperative day 3; Paracentral white cross-shaped infiltrate at corneal cap-stromal bed interface; Corneal cap melting
Lab Findings: Smear revealed Gram-positive cocci; Corneal culture negative

Demographics: 18-year-old male
Chief Complaint: pain and decreased vision
History of Present Illness: The patient underwent bilateral SMILE refractive surgery without intraoperative complications. The day after surgery his uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. On postoperative day 1 he began to experience ocular pain and a reduction in vision. Slit-lamp examination showed small paraxial corneal infiltrates in the right eye and multiple round white stromal infiltrates at the cap-stromal interface in the left eye. Topical antibiotics were increased in frequency and the cap-stromal interface was irrigated with vancomycin on two occasions, but his symptoms worsened and the infiltrates enlarged in both eyes. He was referred to a tertiary center where visual acuity was reduced to light perception and marked photophobia was present. Examination revealed progressive white infiltrates involving the central corneal cap and underlying stroma in the right eye and multiple mid-peripheral infiltrates with diffuse cellular infiltration at the cap-stromal interface in the left eye. Intensive topical antibiotics (levofloxacin, tobramycin) and systemic cefazolin were administered, but the infiltrates continued to advance over the next five days. The corneal caps were surgically enlarged, the caps opened, and the infiltrates were scraped and irrigated with ceftriaxone solution. The right eye showed improvement within two days, while the left eye required repeat irrigation and scraping. One week after the procedures the patient became asymptomatic and the infiltrates began to consolidate and diminish. Topical steroids were introduced a month later and tapered gradually. At six months follow-up the uncorrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/32 in the left eye, with residual stromal scarring noted on slit-lamp examination.
Exposures/Risk Factors: bilateral SMILE refractive surgery
Physical Exam Findings: UCVA 20/20 in both eyes on postoperative day 1; visual acuity light perception in both eyes at referral; marked photophobia; round white infiltrates involving central corneal cap and underlying stromal bed in the right eye; multiple white infiltrates in mid-peripheral area and diffuse cellular infiltration at cap-stromal interface in the left eye; residual stromal scarring in both eyes at six-month follow-up

Demographics: 73-year-old female

Demographics: 41-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels markedly above normal without associated muscle pain or weakness.
History of Present Illness: The patient has a long-standing history of episodic CK elevation attributed to his occupation and sports activities. In his teens he experienced a systemic parasitic infection. He later developed persistent periorbital and facial swelling with mild erythema and skin thickening, which was unresponsive to retinoids and briefly improved with low-dose steroids. At age 40 he noted hoarseness and dysphonia; laryngeal examination revealed lesions that were found to contain intracellular parasites on histology and PCR. He was treated with intravenous therapy targeting the parasite, after which he developed marked hyperCKemia and an increase in serum creatinine, prompting hospital admission for evaluation of a possible inflammatory muscle disease. Immunologic work-up showed reduced IgG, borderline low IgA, normal to borderline high IgM, decreased CD4/CD8 ratio, and low NK and B-cell numbers. Genetic testing identified a hemizygous missense variant in the gene encoding CD40 ligand. Metabolic evaluation revealed a heterozygous missense variant in a gene associated with fatty-acid oxidation–related muscle stress. He was started on immunoglobulin replacement therapy and received antiparasitic treatment, followed by additional therapy for persistent facial swelling. During follow-up a soft-palate lesion was biopsied and diagnosed as an EBV-associated extranodal lymphoma, for which he received chemotherapy and local radiotherapy, achieving complete remission. He remains on immunoglobulin replacement and prophylactic therapy.
Past Medical History: Systemic parasitic infection in childhood; Recurrent otitis media; Childhood bronchopneumonia; Episodes of elevated CK attributed to occupational exposure and boxing; Chronic facial swelling with erythema and skin thickening
Exposures/Risk Factors: Construction work occupation; Travel to Spain and France; Boxing as a recreational activity; Family history of gastric cancer (father) and early-onset lymphoproliferative disease (brother)
Physical Exam Findings: Good general condition; Bilateral orbital/facial swelling
Lab Findings: Creatine kinase >10 times upper limit of normal; Elevated serum creatinine; Serum IgG decreased, IgA borderline low, IgM normal to borderline elevated; Reduced NK cell count; Reduced B-cell count with markedly low switched-memory B cells; CD4+ T-cell count normal, CD8+ slightly elevated, reduced CD4+/CD8+ ratio; Reduced circulating T follicular helper cells; Myositis-associated and specific autoantibodies negative; Complete blood count within normal limits

Demographics: 15-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Fever accompanied with cough for more than 10 days
History of Present Illness: The patient developed fever after a cold more than ten days before admission, with temperature fluctuating between 37 °C and 38 °C, together with cough, fatigue, chills, and sore throat. Symptoms persisted despite administration of a traditional remedy (GanKang). On December 5, 2020 the fever worsened, peaking at 41 °C and was temporarily reduced after oral ibuprofen. He presented to an emergency fever clinic on 5 January 2021. Initial work-up showed low white blood cell count, low hemoglobin, and low platelets. Bone-marrow puncture demonstrated active hematopoietic hyperplasia with otherwise normal three-line proportions and occasional atypical lymphocytes. Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive, ferritin was markedly elevated, and procalcitonin was raised. Imaging showed an enlarged liver and spleen. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was largely unremarkable. Empiric cefoperazone-sulbactam did not improve symptoms, and he was transferred for further evaluation. Vital signs on admission were stable except for a pulse of 110 beats/min. Subsequent laboratory monitoring showed persistent cytopenias, markedly elevated liver enzymes, high LDH, very high ferritin, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, procalcitonin), positive auto-immune antibodies (ANA, anti-Jo-1, rheumatoid factor), and a positive direct Coombs test. The respiratory viral panel detected multiple viruses. Chest CT was normal. Abdominal ultrasound repeatedly documented an enlarged spleen that gradually decreased in size over the hospital stay. The underlying cause of the fever remained uncertain, prompting further infectious disease evaluation.

Demographics: 62-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Cough and chest pain for the last 6 months
History of Present Illness: The patient developed a persistent cough and left-sided chest discomfort that began six months ago. He denied fever, gastrointestinal bleeding, melena, diarrhea, headache, or generalized body aches. He had no prior diagnosis of tuberculosis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or gastroesophageal reflux disease and was not taking any medications. Initial evaluation at a local hospital noted moderate pallor and cachexia but no palpable lymph nodes. Auscultation was unremarkable, and a chest X-ray showed a small left-sided opacity compatible with fluid. Routine blood work revealed low blood cell counts across all lineages and a hemoglobin of 7.7 g/dL with an ESR of 100 mm/h. Tests for tuberculosis (Mantoux, sputum AFB smear and culture) were negative. He was given antitussives and analgesics without significant improvement and was referred for further care. At the referral centre, repeat imaging confirmed the same left-sided opacity. Examination also identified a mild enlargement of the spleen. Liver function tests, coagulation profile, and serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were within normal limits. A reversed albumin/globulin ratio (0.2) prompted a Napier’s aldehyde test, which turned positive. Bone-marrow aspiration demonstrated intracellular and extracellular organisms consistent with a protozoal infection and a slight excess of plasma cells. The patient received intravenous antiprotozoal therapy with rapid clinical and laboratory improvement, and the chest opacity resolved after one month. He remained well on follow-up for six months.
Exposures/Risk Factors: Resident of West Bengal, India; Non-smoker; Non-alcoholic; No recent travel history; No known occupational exposures

Lab Findings: Hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 100 mm/h; Reversed albumin/globulin ratio 0.2; Positive Napier's aldehyde test (serum opacification after 10 minutes); Bone-marrow aspirate showing intracellular and extracellular organisms consistent with a protozoal infection; Slight excess of plasma cells in bone marrow; Negative Mantoux test; Negative sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and culture; Negative hepatitis B surface antigen, anti-HCV, and anti-HIV antibodies; Negative Widal test for enteric fever; Negative malaria antigen test
