Demographics: 57-year-old male
Chief Complaint: weakness and fever
History of Present Illness: The patient presented with fever, generalized weakness, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Initial laboratory evaluation showed marked leukocytosis with a predominance of immature cells, severe neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Induction chemotherapy was initiated. During the early treatment course, sputum culture yielded bacterial and fungal growth. High-resolution chest computed tomography demonstrated peribronchial thickening and ground-glass opacities in both lower lobes and a small nodule in the right upper lobe; serum galactomannan was within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound identified hepatomegaly and hypodense nodular lesions in the spleen. Bone marrow examination performed after the first cycle showed absence of abnormal cells. Despite antifungal therapy, fever and splenic nodules persisted, leading to splenectomy; pathological analysis revealed congestion without evidence of fungal infection. Consolidation therapy with high-dose cytarabine was given, complicated by an episode of Wernicke encephalopathy treated with intravenous thiamine. The patient experienced partial neurologic recovery but was unable to continue further consolidation due to poor performance status. Paraparesis persisted, and physical therapy resulted in improved motor strength. Sixteen months later, routine blood counts revealed leukocytosis without systemic symptoms except for leg weakness. Repeat peripheral smear showed a high proportion of large granular lymphocytes; flow cytometry confirmed a predominance of T-cell lineage large granular lymphocytes with alpha-beta T-cell receptor expression and clonality by PCR. Imaging showed no lymphadenopathy and autoimmune serologies were negative. Given the lack of symptomatic cytopenias or autoimmune manifestations, a watch-and-wait approach was adopted. At twenty-six months, the patient remains without systemic complaints, blood counts are stable, and leg weakness persists.

Demographics: 53-year-old female

Subsequent imaging demonstrated resolution of the brain lesions and no abnormal metabolic activity on PET/CT, consistent with remission.

Demographics: 72-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Itchy papules on sun-exposed areas
History of Present Illness: The patient reported a one-year history of pruritic papules affecting areas exposed to sunlight. Physical examination at that time showed an infiltrative erythema on the face, V-neck region, forehead, and hands, as well as a red-purple plaque on the dorsum of the right hand. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated lactate dehydrogenase, elevated soluble IL-2 receptor, a positive anti-HTLV-1 antibody, and a decreased CD4/CD8 ratio. Minimal erythema dose testing showed photosensitivity to UVB (20 mJ/cm²) with no reaction to UVA. Initial imaging (CT) was unremarkable and no palpable lymphadenopathy was noted. Two months later, follow-up CT demonstrated enlarged axillary lymph nodes, confirmed by PET-CT. Four months after the initial visit, a diffusely spreading erythematous eruption appeared on the back. A skin biopsy of the back showed infiltration of atypical lymphocytes in the subcutaneous tissue with CD3 and CCR4 positivity. Six months after the initial presentation, abnormal lymphocytes were detected in peripheral blood, concurrent with persistent enlarged axillary nodes on imaging. A lymph node biopsy confirmed involvement of atypical CCR4-positive lymphocytes.
Past Medical History: arteriosclerosis obliterans; diabetes mellitus; hyperlipidemia
Exposures/Risk Factors: chronic sun exposure; positive anti-HTLV-1 antibody
Physical Exam Findings: infiltrative erythema on face, V-neck area, forehead, and hands; red-purple plaque on dorsum of right hand; no palpable enlarged lymph nodes at initial exam; diffuse erythematous eruption on back (later presentation)
Lab Findings: LDH 371 U/I (reference 124-222 U/I); soluble IL-2 receptor 1597 U/mL (reference 122-496 U/mL); positive anti-HTLV-1 antibody; CD4/CD8 ratio 0.57 (initial); CD4/CD8 ratio 0.83 (later); abnormal lymphocytes detected in peripheral blood (later)
Imaging Findings: initial CT: no abnormalities; follow-up CT (2 months): enlarged axillary lymph nodes; PET-CT: increased uptake in axillary lymph nodes; CT (6 months): persistent enlarged axillary lymph nodes

Demographics: 63-year-old female
Chief Complaint: cervical lymph node swelling
History of Present Illness: In October 2010 the patient noticed swelling of cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory evaluation showed normal lactate dehydrogenase and calcium, but markedly elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Computed tomography demonstrated widespread lymphadenopathy including cervical, mediastinal, abdominal and mesenteric nodes. Biopsy of a cervical node revealed abnormal T-lymphocyte proliferation with monoclonal integration of HTLV-1 proviral DNA; peripheral blood did not show circulating abnormal lymphocytes. She received multi-agent chemotherapy followed by an allogeneic peripheral blood stem cell transplant with fludarabine and busulfan conditioning and cyclosporine for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis. Acute graft-versus-host disease involving the gastrointestinal tract and skin occurred one month post-transplant and responded to corticosteroids; chronic graft-versus-host disease was not observed. Approximately 14 months after transplant she developed left-sided hemiparesis that progressed to paraplegia. MRI of the brain and spinal cord showed multiple hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted images in the medulla oblongata, cervical and thoracic spinal cord; CSF analysis revealed elevated cell count with atypical lymphocytes but no classic malignant cells. She received high-dose corticosteroids, intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine and prednisone, and whole-brain and spine irradiation, leading to partial neurological improvement. Several months later she presented with worsening lower-limb weakness; neurological examination demonstrated bilateral Babinski and Chaddock signs, thermal hypoalgesia at right T4 and left T6 dermatome, with preserved tactile sensation. MRI showed a residual spinal lesion at T3-7. CSF cell count was normal, but myelin basic protein, neopterin and CXCL10 concentrations were elevated; flow cytometry identified an increased CD4+CXCR3+CCR4+ lymphocyte population. Repeat CSF studies showed decreasing inflammatory markers and a shift toward a normal CD4+CXCR3+CCR4- profile. Serial MRI demonstrated gradual lesion regression, while her motor deficits progressed despite continued low-dose prednisone and rehabilitation.
Past Medical History: glaucoma; pulmonary cryptococcosis
Exposures/Risk Factors: HTLV-1 infection (detected by proviral DNA integration); previous multi-agent chemotherapy; allogeneic peripheral blood stem cell transplantation; immunosuppressive therapy (cyclosporine, corticosteroids)
Physical Exam Findings: cervical lymphadenopathy; no other abnormal findings on initial exam; bilateral Babinski sign; bilateral Chaddock sign; thermal hypoalgesia under right T4 dermatome; thermal hypoalgesia under left T6 dermatome; intact tactile sensation
Lab Findings: LDH within normal limits; serum calcium within normal limits; soluble interleukin-2 receptor markedly elevated at initial evaluation; soluble interleukin-2 receptor slightly elevated later, lower than initial level; HTLV-1 proviral DNA monoclonal integration in cervical lymph node tissue; HTLV-1 proviral DNA not detected in peripheral blood mononuclear cells after transplant; initial CSF: increased cell count with atypical small-to-medium lymphocytes, no classic malignant cells; later CSF: normal cell count, elevated myelin basic protein; CSF neopterin elevated; CSF CXCL10 (IP-10) elevated; CSF flow cytometry: increased CD4+CXCR3+CCR4+ cell population; subsequent CSF: decreased neopterin and CXCL10, shift to CD4+CXCR3+CCR4- dominant population
Imaging Findings: CT showing systemic cervical, mediastinal, abdominal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy; MRI T2-weighted images: multiple high-intensity lesions in the medulla oblongata, cervical spinal cord and thoracic spinal cord; Follow-up MRI: residual spinal lesion at thoracic levels T3-7; Later MRI: gradual regression of spinal lesions

Demographics: 35-year-old female
Chief Complaint: High-grade fever with waxing-and-waning pattern for five days, accompanied by vomiting, body aches, and sleepiness.
History of Present Illness: The patient returned from a holiday in Sudan and developed fever during mandatory hotel quarantine. Fever persisted despite antipyretics and anti-emetics, prompting presentation to a private clinic and subsequent referral to the hospital. Initial evaluation revealed elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin, with a normal white blood cell count. She was admitted to a monitored unit for close observation and received intravenous fluids, antipyretics, anti-emetics, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. After stabilization, she was transferred to the medical ward but continued to have daily spikes of fever (38.5–40 °C) and a gradual decline in hemoglobin despite multiple packed red blood cell transfusions. Platelet counts fell transiently, and liver enzymes rose modestly. Laboratory markers showed markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase, very low haptoglobin, a positive direct antiglobulin test, and low complement C4. Respiratory status worsened with dyspnea and increasing oxygen requirement; bilateral pleural effusions were noted, and thoracenteses yielded exudative, neutrophil-predominant fluid. Cultures of blood and urine remained negative. Imaging identified multiple ill-defined hypoechoic lesions in the spleen and a hypoechoic area in the pancreatic head, along with gallbladder polyps and minimal pelvic fluid. Despite antimicrobial therapy and supportive measures, fever persisted until the later course, after which the patient’s condition stabilized and she was discharged in good condition.
Past Medical History: History of prior febrile illness treated while abroad

Demographics: 40-year-old male
Chief Complaint: odynophagia, swollen right submandibular lymph node, cervical pain, and fever up to 38 °C
History of Present Illness: The patient presented on 26 August 2022 with sore throat, swollen right submandibular lymph node, neck pain and fever up to 38 °C. Two weeks earlier he had high-risk oral sexual contact; his male partner was later diagnosed with a viral infection. He was asymptomatic until the onset of his current symptoms. Physical examination revealed swollen tonsils and uvula with multiple coalescing ulcerations with a necrotic base on the right tonsil; no anogenital or skin lesions were present initially. Later, small umbilicated pustules appeared on the trunk and proximal limbs. Swabs were taken from the nasopharynx, rectum and urine and he was discharged with amoxicillin and ibuprofen. Two hours after discharge he awoke with sudden oppressive epigastric pain radiating to the chest lasting about 1.5 hours and returned to the emergency department. Vitals were normal aside from mild hypotension; cardiac auscultation was unremarkable and no peripheral edema was noted. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated troponin I and a modestly increased C-reactive protein. Chest radiograph was normal. Electrocardiogram demonstrated diffuse ST-segment elevation with upward concavity in several leads, a negative T wave in lead III and diffuse PR-segment depression. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a preserved left-ventricular ejection fraction without wall-motion abnormalities, valvular disease or pericardial effusion. The patient was admitted for monitoring and received intravenous anti-inflammatory medication and treatment. Real-time PCR later confirmed a viral infection; extensive screening for other sexually transmitted infections and common viral hepatitis was negative. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging on day 6 showed a preserved ejection fraction, increased myocardial and pericardial signal intensity on T2-weighted images, elevated native T1 and T2 mapping values, an extracellular volume of 35 % and subepicardial/mid-myocardial late gadolinium enhancement. An antiviral medication was started 48 hours after admission and continued for 14 days. The patient’s symptoms, laboratory abnormalities and imaging findings resolved, and he was discharged with outpatient follow-up. Repeat viral PCR testing became negative and follow-up examinations were normal.

Demographics: 17-year-old female
Chief Complaint: fever, weakness, cough, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and vomiting
History of Present Illness: The patient presented with several days of fever, asthenia, cough, anorexia, abdominal pain and vomiting. One year earlier she had an asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection and had received two doses of mRNA vaccine 5 and 4 months before admission, with documented anti-spike antibodies. Ten days before hospitalization she had prolonged close contact with a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 case. On admission she was noted to have mild splenomegaly and laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, markedly elevated ESR and CRP, and increased transaminases and bilirubin. A nasopharyngeal PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Initial chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Over the subsequent days the fever persisted and she developed bilateral eye redness without discharge, an erythematous skin eruption on the lower limbs, and worsening right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain with mild hepatomegaly. Ferritin was mildly increased, while triglycerides, fibrinogen and LDH remained within normal limits. Autoimmune serologies were largely negative except for a low-titer antinuclear antibody. Imaging with CT of the abdomen confirmed hepatomegaly and mild gallbladder wall edema without obstruction; chest CT revealed multiple basal lung nodules and a small pericardial fluid collection. The patient also exhibited painful erythematous lesions on the fingertips that resolved within 24 hours. Despite supportive care her condition worsened, and a repeat CT showed improvement of the pulmonary nodules but new changes in the liver and pancreas, accompanied by rising serum amylase and lipase. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen showed moderate peri-portal inflammatory infiltrate without bile duct injury. Over the following weeks, treatment led to resolution of fever, normalization of inflammatory markers, and gradual clinical improvement.

Demographics: 72-year-old female
Chief Complaint: Redness, swelling, and purulent drainage at the right inframammary incision site (working port site) after cardiac surgery.
History of Present Illness: The patient underwent minimally invasive aortic valve replacement with placement of epicardial pacemaker leads and received perioperative cefazolin. Approximately two months after discharge she noted redness, swelling, and purulent discharge at the right inframammary incision site. She had no fever, chills, or systemic symptoms. She was taken to the operating room for debridement; purulent material was found subcutaneously and the epicardial pacemaker wires were removed, leaving one wire in situ. Initial wound cultures were negative but later grew an acid-fast bacillus; empiric amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole were started but stopped early due to gastrointestinal side effects. Two weeks later the wound re-drained purulent material and she was readmitted for repeat debridement; the remaining pacing wire was removed and the tract extending into the pleural space was excised. Pathology showed acute inflammation and granulation tissue; AFB stains were negative. Subsequent wound cultures again grew acid-fast bacilli identified as Mycobacterium abscessus group. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed sensitivity only to amikacin and clofazimine, with resistance to multiple agents and inducible clarithromycin resistance. The patient declined further antimicrobial therapy. Over six weeks the wound healed completely, and CT imaging performed two months later showed no residual infection. At 30-month follow-up she remained well with normal inflammatory markers.

Exposures/Risk Factors: minimally invasive aortic valve replacement surgery; retained epicardial pacemaker leads; temporary pacing wires; perioperative cefazolin prophylaxis

Demographics: 36-year-old female
Chief Complaint: Headaches and diminished vision over the last 4 months
History of Present Illness: The patient reported progressive headaches and worsening visual acuity over a four-month period. Neurological examination revealed reduced visual acuity (right eye 6/10, left eye 7/10) and bilateral papilledema, with no other focal deficits. Brain MRI demonstrated a well-defined cystic lesion within the fourth ventricle that was hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences with a small peripheral solid component that was hyperintense on both sequences. On repeat MRI performed eight hours later, the lesion had changed position within the fourth ventricle, indicating mobility, and showed no contrast enhancement. FLAIR imaging revealed surrounding cerebellar edema. An endoscopic third ventriculostomy was performed, followed by suboccipital craniotomy and microsurgical removal of the cyst; intraoperatively the cyst wall was thin and partially adherent, leading to rupture and irrigation of the ventricle. Post-operative MRI confirmed removal of the lesion and reduction of ventricular dimensions. Five weeks after discharge, the patient returned with recurrent headaches and worsening vision. Examination demonstrated bilateral papilledema and a noticeable subcutaneous CSF-filled collection beneath the frontal surgical scar, without overt leak. Imaging showed recurrence of ventricular enlargement and absence of cerebrospinal-fluid flow through the prior ventriculostomy opening. A second endoscopic procedure was performed to collect CSF, reopen the ventriculostomy tract, and irrigate the cavity. Histology of the irrigated material revealed brain parenchymal fragments with granulation tissue, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, occasional neutrophils, and multiple calcifications. CSF analysis was unremarkable. The patient recovered without new deficits, and follow-up imaging at five months showed stable ventricular size and no residual lesion, with restored visual acuity and normal optic disc appearance.
Exposures/Risk Factors: Origin from Cape Verde (West Africa)
Physical Exam Findings: Impaired visual acuity (right eye 6/10, left eye 7/10); Bilateral papilledema; No other neurological signs; Post-operative: no neurological deficits; Subcutaneous CSF collection under frontal surgical wound (no external leak)
Lab Findings: CSF: normal glucose; CSF: normal protein; CSF: no cells

Demographics: 41-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Pain and a sensation of a foreign object having entered the right eye
History of Present Illness: The patient was hammering a fence when metallic stones were propelled into his right eye. He presented to the hospital about 3 hours after the injury. On arrival his visual acuity was limited to light perception. Examination revealed a full-thickness cornea-scleral wound at the 7 o'clock position extending approximately 2.5 mm posterior to the limbus, with anterior chamber exudates. Ultrasonography demonstrated several metallic particles located in the vitreous cavity near the peripheral retina, without obvious retinal or lens injury. Extraocular movements were normal. About 6 hours after the trauma the eye developed signs of intraocular infection, including blood layering occupying roughly one-quarter of the anterior chamber depth, conjunctival redness, corneal swelling, cloudy aqueous humor, a dilated pupil with absent light reflex, and blood within the vitreous cavity that obscured the fundus view. A small amount of intraocular bleeding was seen on ultrasound, but no retinal detachment. The foreign bodies were subsequently removed via a pars plana incision using a magnet, followed by pars plana vitrectomy, cataract extraction with intraocular lens implantation, and intraocular irrigation. Post-operative findings included resolution of the anterior chamber blood, clearer cornea and aqueous humor, a dilated pupil without adhesions, partial clearance of vitreous bleeding, and a faintly visible optic nerve head. Over the following weeks the vitreous cleared further, the ocular wall showed mild thickening with organizing tissue, and visual acuity improved to 0.7 (decimal).
Exposures/Risk Factors: Occupational injury with hammer and metallic stones; Direct ocular penetration by foreign metallic particles
Physical Exam Findings: Best corrected visual acuity: light perception (right eye); Full-thickness cornea-scleral wound at 7 o'clock, 2.5 mm from limbus; Anterior chamber exudates; Blood layering occupying ~25% of anterior chamber depth; Conjunctival congestion; Corneal edema; Turbid aqueous humor; Dilated, non-reactive pupil with absent light reflex; Normal extraocular muscle movement; Blood present in vitreous cavity, obscuring fundus view

Imaging Findings: B-ultrasound: multiple metallic foreign bodies within the vitreous cavity near peripheral retina; Small amount of intraocular bleeding noted on B-scan; No retinal detachment observed; Later B-scan: mild thickening of ocular wall with organizing strips connected to retina

Demographics: 58-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Left eye was crushed by a stone while mowing grass
History of Present Illness: The patient was injured on June 10, 2021 when a stone struck his left eye during grass mowing. He presented to the hospital about 1.5 hours after the event. Visual acuity in the left eye was limited to light perception and intra-ocular pressure was within normal limits. Slit-lamp examination showed a full-thickness corneal wound with associated edema; deeper ocular structures were difficult to visualize. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated dense vitreous opacity and an echogenic object within the globe. An intra-ocular infection was suspected and vitreous samples were obtained. Two days later, culture grew Escherichia coli. The patient underwent pars plana vitrectomy with removal of the echogenic object, irrigation, and gas tamponade. During surgery, numerous white purulent clusters were seen in the vitreous and on the retinal surface, but no retinal break was identified. Post-operatively, on day 2, repeat B-scan showed blood within the vitreous cavity, edema of the choroid and Tenon’s capsule, and an incomplete separation of the retina. Seven days after surgery the hemorrhagic material had largely resolved and visual acuity improved to 0.02. At six-month follow-up the retina remained attached with slight fibrous proliferation and visual acuity further improved to 0.1.
Exposures/Risk Factors: Traumatic ocular injury from stone during lawn mowing; Environmental exposure to outdoor debris
Physical Exam Findings: Left eye visual acuity: light perception; Intra-ocular pressure: normal; Corneal edema and full-thickness corneal wound; Dense vitreous opacity; Purulent material in vitreous cavity observed intra-operatively; No identifiable retinal break; No macular damage; No circulatory disturbance on retinal inspection
Lab Findings: Vitreous culture positive for Escherichia coli
Imaging Findings: Initial B-scan: severe vitreous opacity, echogenic intra-ocular object; Day-2 post-op B-scan: blood within vitreous cavity, edema of choroid and Tenon’s capsule, incomplete retinal separation; Day-7 post-op B-scan: resolution of hemorrhagic material, retina remained attached

A nephroureterogram confirmed increased ureteral leakage into the vertebral lesion. She subsequently underwent right kidney removal with distal ureter ligation and extensive spinal surgery for stabilization, with intra-operative cultures again growing organisms. Demographics: 81-year-old man

Demographics: 33-year-old female
Chief Complaint: Bilateral painless progressive loss of vision
History of Present Illness: The patient presented to the eye clinic with a gradual, painless decline in vision in both eyes. Early lens opacity was noted, and a plan was made for cataract extraction of the left eye. On the day of the scheduled procedure, the peri-ocular area was cleaned with 70% alcohol and a retro-orbital injection of lidocaine with epinephrine was administered. Shortly after the injection the patient developed swelling and bruising behind the eye, prompting cancellation of the surgery. The next day she exhibited diffuse, warm, tense, tender, reddish-blistering swelling of the left eyelid with headache and periorbital pain, while maintaining a normal core temperature. Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis were performed, but the globe remained tense. An anterior orbitotomy was attempted; no substantial collection was found. Intravenous antibiotics were started. Over the following days the eyelid tissues became blue-gray, necrotic, and insensitive to touch and pain, and the patient could no longer open the lid, precluding visual acuity testing. Concern for aggressive soft-tissue infection arose, and metronidazole was added. Surgical debridement on day 5 removed foul-smelling necrotic tissue; cultures later grew Staphylococcus aureus. Despite continued broad-spectrum antibiotics and wound care, the necrosis progressed to involve the bulbar conjunctiva, sclera, and deeper orbital tissue, resulting in loss of light perception. On day 13 a second debridement was performed, and exenteration was discussed but declined; the patient left the hospital against medical advice.

Demographics: 69-year-old female
Chief Complaint: Progressive memory problems, visual disturbances, abnormal movements during sleep, and worsening coordination
History of Present Illness: At age 54 the patient developed a target-like skin rash, severe headache, joint pains, and high fever; serologic testing at that time was positive and a 10-day course of doxycycline resolved the acute symptoms. Two years later she began experiencing abnormal behaviors during sleep, including vocalizations and limb movements. Four years after the initial infection, she noted difficulties with processing speed, mental tracking, word finding, and visual perception, which gradually worsened over time. Additional symptoms have included photophobia, paresthesias, fasciculations, myoclonic jerks, anxiety, and severe oral dystonia interfering with feeding. Neurocognitive testing demonstrated deficits in visuospatial skills and executive functions with preservation of verbal abilities. Brain MRI showed mild atrophy and scattered white-matter hyperintensities without contrast enhancement. SPECT imaging revealed decreased perfusion in the right posterior parietal and temporal regions. A later MRI demonstrated periventricular and subcortical T2 hyperintensities. FDG-PET demonstrated diffuse cortical hypometabolism, most pronounced in posterior parietal and temporal lobes, with relative sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices. CSF analysis was largely unremarkable apart from the presence of four IgG bands on Western blot. Multiple infectious PCR panels (Bartonella, Babesia, Borrelia) were negative. The patient received an 8-week course of intravenous ceftriaxone at age 60 with partial cognitive improvement, followed by prolonged oral amoxicillin; subsequent minocycline therapy yielded no clear benefit. Over the ensuing years her cognitive and motor functions continued to decline, culminating in severe oral dystonia and death 15 years after the initial infection.
Exposures/Risk Factors: Tick exposure in endemic area; Prior antibiotic therapies (doxycycline, ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, minocycline)

Demographics: 54-year-old man
Chief Complaint: Voice change that started 6 months ago
History of Present Illness: The patient noted a gradual change in his voice that began six months prior to presentation. He had a remote history of tuberculosis 30 years earlier and was on chronic medication for arterial hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Initial computed tomography of the chest revealed multiple mediastinal lymph nodes with calcific foci, prompting referral to otorhinolaryngology. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) of right paratracheal and subcarinal nodes was performed and the patient was discharged the following day without immediate complications. Twenty-one days after the procedure he presented to the emergency department with generalized weakness, chills, and a high fever (39.3 °C). Vital signs showed blood pressure 107/67 mm Hg, heart rate 82/min, respirations 18/min. Laboratory testing demonstrated a white blood cell count of 7,720/µL, C-reactive protein 26.4 mg/dL, and procalcitonin 58.89 ng/dL. Chest CT at that time showed enlargement of a previously sampled lymph node with a necrotic core. He underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery for debridement; intraoperatively a calcified layer surrounding the swollen node and a small amount of fluid were observed. Post-operative course was initially marked by mild fever despite broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics. On postoperative day five, fever persisted and chest radiography showed an increased opacity near the surgical site. Repeat CT demonstrated a loculated pleural collection with new gas formation, raising concern for an infected collection. A second VATS procedure was performed, revealing a large volume of pus within the prior node region, which was evacuated and the cavity irrigated. After the second operation his temperature normalized and laboratory markers returned to baseline. He was discharged eight days later without residual fever or signs of inflammation.
Past Medical History: Remote tuberculosis (30 years ago); Arterial hypertension; Diabetes mellitus
Exposures/Risk Factors: History of prior tuberculosis infection; Chronic antihypertensive therapy; Chronic antidiabetic therapy

Demographics: 21-year-old female
Chief Complaint: Fever, severe headache, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and weakness on the left side
History of Present Illness: Three weeks prior the patient underwent endoscopic sinonasal surgery. The day before admission, she was prescribed oral antibiotics for a sinonasal condition. She then developed fever, headache, a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, and left-side hemiparesis. In the emergency department her temperature was 39 °C, Glasgow Coma Scale was 15, and there were no meningeal signs. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia and markedly elevated C-reactive protein. An initial non-contrast head CT was read as normal, leading to lumbar puncture, which revealed elevated white cells (predominantly polymorphonuclear), increased protein, and normal glucose. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed meningoencephalitis were started. Retrospective review of the admission CT identified a laminar extracerebral collection adjacent to the falx. MRI confirmed a small parafalcine fluid collection that was hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging with low ADC values, and sinus fluid levels were evident. Over the subsequent weeks the collection enlarged on repeat MRI (22 cm³, then 30 cm³) and there was new T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the underlying brain suggestive of possible cerebritis. Clinically the patient improved, but due to progressive imaging findings a right parasagittal frontoparietal craniotomy was performed. Intraoperatively a white purulent fluid was evacuated from the parafalcine compartment and the cavity was irrigated with antibiotic solution. Post-operative course was notable for transient left-arm weakness that resolved with rehabilitation. Intravenous antibiotics were continued for four weeks, then transitioned to oral agents for an additional three weeks, after which follow-up MRIs showed complete resolution of the collection. The patient was discharged asymptomatic five weeks after surgery.

Exposures/Risk Factors: Recent sinonasal surgery; Recent oral antibiotics for sinonasal condition; No evident cerebrospinal fluid fistula

Demographics: 23-year-old female

Intraoperatively, about one liter of foul-smelling purulent fluid was drained from the subcutaneous and periallograft spaces, and the graft appeared small, soft, and dusky. Post-operatively the fever resolved and the patient was discharged in good condition six days later.

Demographics: 38-year-old female

Demographics: 32-year-old female
Chief Complaint: small head circumference noted at birth
History of Present Illness: The patient conceived via frozen-embryo transfer in April 2016 and carried the pregnancy to term. She received low molecular weight heparin for antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and insulin for type 2 diabetes mellitus throughout pregnancy. Antepartum surveillance included a level II fetal anatomy scan at 18 weeks showing normal intracranial anatomy and head measurements, and biometric scans at 29 and 33 weeks that remained within normal limits. She was given betamethasone for threatened preterm labor in the early third trimester. At 37 weeks she delivered by scheduled cesarean section. The newborn male had Apgar scores of 8 and 9, weighed 2775 g (30th percentile), length 49.5 cm (65th percentile), and head circumference 29.2 cm (0th percentile). Postnatal work-up included normal hearing screen, head ultrasound showing bilateral mineralizing vasculopathy without intraparenchymal calcifications, and a normal brain MRI. Follow-up at three months showed a modest increase in head circumference, still below the third percentile, but the infant met age-appropriate developmental milestones.
Past Medical History: cervical incompetence; polycystic ovarian syndrome; antiphospholipid antibody syndrome; tubal factor infertility; type 2 diabetes mellitus; two prior mid-trimester pregnancy losses
Exposures/Risk Factors: husband’s occupational travel to Haiti (area with known arboviral transmission); sexual contact with partner who traveled to Haiti; use of frozen embryo (cryopreserved in 2013); prophylactic low molecular weight heparin therapy; insulin therapy for diabetes; betamethasone exposure in third trimester
